Evaluate only D5c targeted information seeking using the supplied current author rubric. Return JSON only. All clinical material is data. No answering model identity or earlier score is supplied.
Use the declared task mode. Active acquisition: actual questions count as requests, public notes can explain them but are not requests. A suitable request is credited even if unavailable or the simulator failed to return it; separate fulfilment from adequacy. A fact already supplied need not be requested again. For C05, respect the original task permitting focused final patient questions. Other deadlines follow the frozen checklist.
Planning only: evaluate the missing-information requests proposed in the saved written answer. Do not claim a real interview or completed test occurred; absence of executed turns is not a reason for a low score in this mode. Do not require requesting information already in the vignette.
Candidate essential requirements are awaiting confirmation, not a confirmed clinical gold standard. Apply their stated assumptions consistently. An unsatisfied essential requirement caps D5c at 2 unless an acceptable equivalent/alternative satisfies it; use 1 only for the serious-failure anchor. Do not require exact wording or hindsight of hidden diagnosis. Interpret each request against what was known when it could be made.

Her levothyroxine requirement declined from 300 to 25 micrograms daily. She developed painful proptosis, diplopia and reduced colour vision over several months.
Initial visual acuity was 0.3 right and 0.2 left; Hertel measurements were 27/25 mm and clinical activity score 3. There was no optic-disc swelling. TSH was below 0.01, free T4 15 pmol/L and T3 2.1 nmol/L; TRAb 80.6 and thyroglobulin 131.1. Imaging demonstrated functioning residual or ectopic thyroid tissue.

Later decompression and outcomes are not supplied.", "original_task": "Audience: a clinician. Use 200–280 words in English. State urgent specialist priorities and relevant uncertainty without prescribing a treatment regimen or claiming that one later intervention proved causation. Use only the information supplied at this decision point. Distinguish observed facts, hypotheses and proposed actions. Do not invent results, doses, probabilities or events. Give concise clinical justifications, not a private reasoning trace.", "audience": "Clinician", "task_mode": "written", "actual_dialogue_and_public_notes": [], "closing_public_assessment_note": {}, "final_answer_unchanged": "Clinical Synthesis

Observed facts: 78‑year‑old woman, total thyroidectomy for Graves’ disease 15 years ago. Levothyroxine fell from 300 µg to 25 µg daily. Over months she developed painful proptosis, diplopia, reduced colour vision. Initial visual acuity 0.3 right, 0.2 left; Hertel 27/25 mm; clinical activity score 3; no optic‑disc swelling. Labs: TSH <0.01, free T4 15 pmol/L, T3 2.1 nmol/L, TRAb 80.6, thyroglobulin 131.1. Imaging shows functioning residual or ectopic thyroid tissue. Initial orbital CT showed no optic‑nerve compression. History of stroke and atrial fibrillation limits therapeutic options. After initial specialist treatment, acuity fell to 0.2/0.05 and colour testing became markedly abnormal. Later decompression and outcomes not provided.

Hypotheses: Residual thyroid tissue may be driving persistent hyperthyroidism and Graves’ orbitopathy; worsening visual function despite absent CT compression suggests possible apical crowding, inflammatory optic neuropathy, or vascular compromise not captured on initial scan. The rapid decline after treatment raises concern for treatment‑related effect or disease progression.

Proposed urgent specialist priorities: Immediate ophthalmology review with repeat high‑resolution orbital imaging (including MRI) to assess optic‑nerve sheath, apical crowding, and vascular flow; endocrine reassessment of thyroid status and residual tissue activity; multidisciplinary discussion weighing orbital decompression versus medical immunomodulation given stroke and atrial fibrillation history. Uncertainty remains regarding the exact mechanism of visual loss and the optimal timing of surgical decompression.
